title: Role of nutrition in performance enhancement and postexercise recovery
publisher: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine (Dovepress)
claims: Carbohydrate loading aims to maximise muscle glycogen before endurance exercise lasting longer than 90 minutes; reported benefits include delaying fatigue by about 20% and improving performance by 2% to 3%.

The original loading protocol used three days of intense training with low carbohydrate intake followed by three days of reduced training with high carbohydrate intake; later work showed the depletion phase was unnecessary and that 24 hours may be enough to maximise glycogen stores.

There appears to be no advantage to increasing pre-exercise muscle glycogen for moderate-intensity cycling or running lasting 60 to 90 minutes, because significant glycogen remains in the muscle after exercise.
For exercise lasting less than 90 minutes, 7 to 12 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body mass should be consumed in the 24 hours before exercise.
For exercise longer than 60 minutes, 1 to 4 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body mass are recommended in the 1 to 4 hours before exercise.

Glucose absorption through SGLT1 saturates at approximately 1 gram per minute; adding fructose, absorbed through GLUT5, raises exogenous carbohydrate oxidation to approximately 1.3 grams per minute, with performance benefits appearing in the third hour of exercise.

Recommendations reflect the absorption limit: 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour from multiple sources for events longer than 2.5 hours, and 60 grams per hour from single or multiple sources for exercise lasting 2 to 3 hours.
